topic: Linux Kernel and Operating Systems Internals

concepts.title: System Call Mechanics: Sysenter, Syscall, and Ring Transitions
concepts.content: A system call switches the CPU from unprivileged ring 3 to ring 0 kernel space using the 'syscall' or 'sysenter' instruction. The kernel loads 'entry_SYSCALL_64', saves registers into 'struct pt_regs' on the per-thread kernel stack, and dispatches via 'sys_call_table'. Beware: frequent user-to-kernel boundary crossings incur cache eviction overhead and context-switching penalties.
concepts.image_prompt: Layered stack diagram: User Ring 3 (glibc syscall wrapper) points down via 'syscall instruction' arrow to Kernel Ring 0 (entry_SYSCALL_64), branching to pt_regs stack save, then sys_call_table dispatch, returning via 'sysret'.

concepts.title: Task Struct: The Monolithic Process Descriptor
concepts.content: The kernel models every process and thread as a 'struct task_struct' allocated via the slab allocator. It encapsulates PID, thread group ID 'tgid', execution state, credentials, and pointers to 'mm_struct' and 'files_struct'. Threads share 'mm_struct' while processes hold distinct virtual memory maps. Trap: deep pointer chasing across task structures triggers severe L1/L2 data cache misses in tight monitoring loops.
concepts.image_prompt: Tree diagram: struct task_struct root node links via arrows to mm_struct (virtual memory), files_struct (descriptor table), signal_struct, and cred (UID/GID credentials), with distinct thread pointers sharing the same mm_struct.

concepts.title: Process Creation: clone3, Copy-on-Write, and pidfd
concepts.content: Modern process spawning uses 'clone3(2)' with 'struct clone_args', deprecating legacy 'fork()'. Setting 'CLONE_VM' creates a thread, while omitting it lazily duplicates page tables via Copy-on-Write (CoW). Specifying 'CLONE_PIDFD' returns a stable file descriptor to avoid PID recycling race conditions. Trap: heavy write operations immediately after cloning trigger catastrophic CoW page-fault storms across large parent address spaces.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline diagram: clone3 call with struct clone_args flows right to kernel copy_process, branching into shared memory thread path via CLONE_VM or Copy-on-Write page table duplication, outputting an unforgeable pidfd descriptor.

concepts.title: Context Switching: __switch_to and Hardware State Transition
concepts.content: When rescheduling, 'context_switch()' updates the memory context via 'switch_mm_irqs_off()' and calls '__switch_to_asm()' for register state. It switches the kernel stack pointer 'RSP', updates the Thread Local Storage base via 'FS_BASE', and restores callee-saved registers. If switching address spaces, updating 'CR3' invalidates non-global TLB entries. Trap: high context switch frequency degrades CPU pipelines and pollutes instruction caches.
concepts.image_prompt: State diagram: Task A running transitions via scheduler pick to switch_mm (CR3 reload and TLB flush), flowing down to __switch_to_asm (RSP exchange, FS_BASE reload, and register restoration), activating Task B.

concepts.title: CPU Scheduling: EEVDF Latency and Eligibility Engine
concepts.content: Linux replaced CFS with Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First (EEVDF) in 6.6+. EEVDF tracks task virtual time 'vruntime' and assigns a virtual deadline based on requested latency tolerance slice via 'sched_setattr()'. Tasks become eligible only when their allocation lag is zero or positive. Trap: setting improper latency sensitivity or miscalculating nice levels starves throughput-bound batch workloads.
concepts.image_prompt: Timeline diagram: Time axis shows task Virtual Runtime versus Eligibility Time. Runnable entities queue into an eligible red-black tree, ordered by Virtual Deadline arrow pointing to current CPU execution dispatch.

concepts.title: Real-Time Scheduling: SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR, and Priority Inversion
concepts.content: Real-time classes 'SCHED_FIFO' and 'SCHED_RR' preempt fair tasks with priorities 1 to 99. To prevent unbonded priority inversion where low-priority tasks hold locks needed by high-priority tasks, the kernel uses 'rt_mutex' priority inheritance. Warning: a runaway FIFO thread running an infinite loop starves all fair tasks, requiring emergency enforcement via '/proc/sys/kernel/sched_rt_runtime_us' (default 950000 µs).
concepts.image_prompt: State diagram: Low-priority Task holds mutex; High-priority Task blocks on mutex; rt_mutex temporarily boosts Low-priority Task to High-priority level, pointing execution arrow past Medium-priority Task to unlock and restore priority.

concepts.title: Deterministic Latency: The Mainline PREEMPT_RT Architecture
concepts.content: Merged into mainline in Linux 6.12, 'CONFIG_PREEMPT_RT' converts standard spinlocks into sleeping 'rt_mutex' locks and forces softirqs into preemptible kernel threads. Critical sections that previously disabled preemption now yield to higher-priority real-time threads, capping scheduling jitter to microseconds. Trade-off: overall peak system throughput drops roughly 5-15% due to increased lock tracking and context switch overhead.
concepts.image_prompt: Comparison matrix: Left column shows Standard Kernel with non-preemptible raw spinlocks and blocked interrupt threads; Right column shows PREEMPT_RT with sleeping rt_mutex locks, preemptible critical sections, and threaded softirq queues.

concepts.title: Extensible Scheduling: sched_ext (SCX) BPF Framework
concepts.content: Merged in Linux 6.12, 'sched_ext' allows implementing CPU scheduling algorithms using sandboxed eBPF programs loaded dynamically without rebooting. Tasks enqueue through BPF dispatch queues (DSQs) via the 'sched_ext_ops' callback table. A hardware watchdog automatically unloads faulty schedulers and reverts to EEVDF if tasks stall. Failure mode: buggy dispatch logic that starves critical user threads triggers watchdog timeouts.
concepts.image_prompt: Layered stack diagram: Core Kernel scheduler class delegates to sched_ext framework, passing task wakeups to BPF Scheduler Program via sched_ext_ops, pushing runnable tasks into BPF Dispatch Queues (DSQ) to CPU cores.

concepts.title: Multiprocessor Scheduling: Energy Aware Scheduling and PELT
concepts.content: Energy Aware Scheduling (EAS) operates on asymmetric Arm big.LITTLE and DynamIQ architectures. It couples Per-Entity Load Tracking (PELT) with kernel Energy Models to calculate the optimal balance between performance and power consumption. The 'schedutil' governor reads PELT utilization metrics to set CPU frequencies. Trap: erratic, bursty compute spikes confuse PELT decay windows, causing delayed frequency ramp-ups.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline diagram: Task runnable signal enters PELT utilization accumulator, feeding into Energy Model calculator comparing Little core versus Big core power costs, routing task to optimal core via Schedutil frequency governor.

concepts.title: Virtual Memory: 5-Level Paging and TLB Shootdowns
concepts.content: X86-64 uses multi-level hierarchical paging—PGD, P4D, PUD, PMD, and PTE—translating 48-bit (4-level) or 57-bit (5-level via 'CONFIG_X86_5LEVEL') virtual addresses into physical frames. The MMU caches translations in the TLB. When a page table mapping changes, the kernel issues inter-processor interrupts (IPIs) for TLB shootdowns. Trap: high shootdown rates on 128+ core systems trigger severe interconnect stalls.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline diagram: 57-bit Virtual Address divides into five index segments (PGD, P4D, PUD, PMD, PTE) pointing sequentially through table blocks to Physical Page Frame, showing TLB cache check and IPI shootdown broadcast.

concepts.title: Kernel Isolation: Kernel Page Table Isolation (KPTI)
concepts.content: KPTI mitigates Meltdown by separating user-space and kernel-space page tables. In user mode, the CR3 register points to a shadow page table containing user mappings and only minimal kernel trampolines for interrupt entry. Transitioning to kernel mode reloads CR3 with the full mapping. Trade-off: dual-CR3 reloading invalidates TLB entries and introduces 5-30% performance penalties on syscall-intensive I/O.
concepts.image_prompt: Comparison matrix: Left diagram shows User CR3 table with mapped user memory and tiny kernel entry trampoline; Right diagram shows Kernel CR3 table with full user memory plus full kernel space mapping.

concepts.title: Physical Page Management: The Buddy Allocator and Zones
concepts.content: The physical memory manager divides RAM into NUMA nodes and zones ('ZONE_DMA', 'ZONE_NORMAL', 'ZONE_MOVABLE'). Memory allocations request power-of-two page blocks (order-0 to order-10) using 'alloc_pages()'. When blocks are freed, the buddy allocator merges adjacent free blocks of identical order. Failure mode: external memory fragmentation exhausts high-order contiguous blocks even when gigabytes of total order-0 memory remain free.
concepts.image_prompt: Tree diagram: 64KB Order-4 memory block splits downwards into two 32KB Order-3 buddies, further splitting into 16KB Order-2 blocks; reverse arrows show Buddy Allocator merging adjacent free blocks back into contiguous parent blocks.

concepts.title: Slab Allocation: SLUB Memory Allocator and Caches
concepts.content: The SLUB allocator provisions small, fixed-size kernel objects without buddy allocator page waste. It serves allocations via named caches like 'dentry' and 'inode_cache', or generic 'kmalloc-X' buckets. SLUB eliminates per-CPU queues in favor of page freelist pointers. Trap: buffer overflows overwriting freelist metadata trigger kernel panics, mitigated by hardening options like 'CONFIG_SLAB_FREELIST_HARDENED'.
concepts.image_prompt: Layered stack diagram: Page frame managed by SLUB divides into contiguous fixed-size object slots, with an active freelist pointer linking free slots sequentially, pointing up to kmem_cache and kmalloc request endpoints.

concepts.title: Modern Page Abstraction: Memory Folios and Compound Pages
concepts.content: The kernel transitioned from legacy 'struct page' arrays to 'struct folio' to manage arbitrary-sized contiguous physical memory blocks safely. A folio guarantees it represents the head page of a memory allocation, eliminating ambiguity between head and tail pages. Trap: passing raw page pointers across old filesystem drivers risks subtle memory corruption if drivers assume order-0 4KB pages.
concepts.image_prompt: Comparison matrix: Left side shows Legacy Compound Page with confusing head/tail pointer flags; Right side shows Modern struct folio wrapping multi-page contiguous chunks (4KB, 16KB, 64KB) as a single typed object.

concepts.title: Memory Eviction: Multi-Gen LRU (MGLRU) Architecture
concepts.content: MGLRU replaces the traditional dual active/inactive LRU queues with generational rings, tracking page coldness via generation numbers. The page table scanner increments generations based on page access bits, avoiding lock contention and minimizing kswapd CPU utilization. Trap: misconfiguring generation aging rates via '/sys/kernel/mm/lru_gen/min_ttl_ms' causes aggressive eviction of latency-critical shared libraries.
concepts.image_prompt: Loop diagram: Generational ring buffer showing Gen 0 (oldest/coldest pages), Gen 1, Gen 2, and Gen 3 (newest/hottest pages); aging pointer moves forward while kswapd evicts cold pages from Gen 0 to swap.

concepts.title: Kernel Memory Reclaiming: kswapd, Watermarks, and ZRAM
concepts.content: Memory reclamation triggers when free pages dip below zone watermarks: Wmark_Min, Wmark_Low, and Wmark_High. The 'kswapd' daemon wakes at Wmark_Low and reclaims pages until reaching Wmark_High. If allocation breaches Wmark_Min, threads enter synchronous Direct Reclaim, freezing execution. Use ZRAM with 'zstd' compression to store swapped pages in RAM, avoiding slow disk thrashing during memory pressure spikes.
concepts.image_prompt: Gauge panel diagram: Vertical memory levels showing Wmark_High, Wmark_Low, and Wmark_Min watermarks; kswapd activates between High and Low, while Direct Reclaim stall activates below Wmark_Min, routing pages to ZRAM compressed store.

concepts.title: Autonomous Memory Monitoring: DAMON and DAMOS Subsystem
concepts.content: The Data Access Monitor (DAMON) samples virtual and physical memory access patterns using adaptive region-based scanning, maintaining near-zero CPU overhead. Paired with DAMOS (DAMON-based Operation Schemes), administrators automate memory policies like proactive page migration between CXL tiers or cold memory madvise reclamation. Trap: setting sampling intervals too aggressively causes excessive TLB flush interrupts.
concepts.image_prompt: Loop diagram: Monitored memory space divided into dynamic regions; DAMON sampler detects access frequency, feeding access heatmap into DAMOS policy engine, which triggers proactive MADV_PAGEOUT or NUMA/CXL migration actions.

concepts.title: Virtual Memory Allocation: On-Demand Demand Paging and CoW
concepts.content: Calling 'mmap()' or 'brk()' does not allocate physical memory immediately; it only creates or modifies a Virtual Memory Area ('vm_area_struct'). When the process accesses the address, the CPU triggers a page fault (vector 14). 'handle_mm_fault()' allocates a physical page, zeroes it, and updates PTEs. Trap: overcommitting memory via 'vm.overcommit_memory=1' leads to sudden OOM killer termination when pages are dirtied.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline diagram: Process executes memory write to unmapped address, triggering Page Fault (Vector 14); kernel handle_mm_fault allocates physical page frame, updates Page Table Entry (PTE), and resumes user instruction.

concepts.title: User-Space Memory Trapping: userfaultfd Mechanics
concepts.content: The 'userfaultfd' system call allows user-space daemons to handle page faults for designated memory regions. Upon an unmapped access, the kernel halts the faulting thread and delivers an event descriptor to user space. The monitor fetches data from the network and injects it via 'UFFDIO_COPY'. Common pitfall: deadlocks occur if the userfaultfd polling daemon itself attempts to access monitored memory.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline diagram: Faulting thread hits unmapped page, kernel traps fault and sends userfaultfd event to user-space monitor daemon; monitor loads page via network/storage and invokes UFFDIO_COPY to unblock the faulting thread.

concepts.title: VMA Management: The Maple Tree Data Structure
concepts.content: The Linux kernel replaced the red-black tree with the Maple Tree for tracking process Virtual Memory Areas (VMAs). Maple Tree is a B-tree variant designed for range locking and RCU-safe lookups, significantly reducing 'mmap_lock' contention during concurrent page faults. Trap: high multi-threaded memory allocation rates can still experience lock latency if writer threads hold write semaphores.
concepts.image_prompt: Tree diagram: Maple Tree B-tree structure displaying range intervals [Start, End] across nodes; read-side locks traverse down concurrently using RCU, while write updates perform localized split-and-balance operations.

concepts.title: Memory Ordering: Memory Barriers and Weak Architecture Models
concepts.content: Modern superscalar CPUs reorder memory reads and writes to maximize throughput. On weak memory architectures like ARM64 and RISC-V, the kernel uses 'smp_mb()', 'smp_rmb()', and 'smp_wmb()' or acquire/release semantics ('smp_load_acquire', 'smp_store_release') to guarantee visibility. Failure mode: missing memory barriers in lockless multi-core shared data structures cause intermittent, unreproducible stale-read race bugs.
concepts.image_prompt: Timeline diagram: CPU 0 writes Data followed by smp_store_release(Flag); Memory interconnect enforces order; CPU 1 reads Flag via smp_load_acquire, guaranteeing subsequent read of Data retrieves the updated value.

concepts.title: Kernel Concurrency: Queued Spinlocks (qspinlock)
concepts.content: Standard test-and-set spinlocks flood the CPU cache interconnect with bus invalidations under contention. Linux uses queued spinlocks ('qspinlock'), assigning contending CPU cores into per-CPU MCS array queues. Cores spin locally on their own cache lines until their ticket is called. Trap: calling a function that sleeps while holding a spinlock results in immediate 'BUG: scheduling while atomic'.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline diagram: Contending CPU cores 1, 2, and 3 enqueue into per-CPU MCS queue nodes; Lock owner holds lock while queued cores spin locally on private cache lines; release transfers ownership via atomic CAS.

concepts.title: Sleepable Locks: Mutex Fast-Path and Wound-Wait Mutexes
concepts.content: Linux 'struct mutex' uses an atomic compare-and-swap fast-path: if uncontended, locking requires zero kernel intervention. Under contention, it enters adaptive spinning if the owner is actively running on another CPU, avoiding sleep latency. Complex multi-lock graphics drivers use wound-wait mutexes ('ww_mutex') with acquire contexts to detect and resolve potential deadlocks automatically through transaction backoffs.
concepts.image_prompt: State diagram: Mutex acquire attempts atomic cmpxchg fast-path; on failure, checks if owner is running (adaptive spin); if owner sleeps, enqueues onto wait_list and puts thread to sleep; ww_mutex path rolls back on deadlock.

concepts.title: Lockless Synchronization: Read-Copy-Update (RCU)
concepts.content: RCU provides lock-free read access to shared dynamic data structures. Readers execute within 'rcu_read_lock()' and 'rcu_read_unlock()' without taking locks or atomic operations. Writers make a private copy, update it, atomically swap pointers via 'rcu_assign_pointer()', and defer reclaiming old memory via 'synchronize_rcu()' until all readers pass a quiescent state. Failure mode: sleeping inside an RCU read-side critical section wedges the grace-period engine.
concepts.image_prompt: Timeline diagram: Old data version pointer active; Writer swaps pointer to New Copy; Grace Period begins; concurrent Readers finish reading Old version; once all readers reach Quiescent State, old memory is reclaimed.

concepts.title: Lockless Reads: Sequence Counters and Seqlocks
concepts.content: Seqlocks protect small data structures where writers must never be starved by frequent readers. Writers increment a sequence counter via 'write_seqlock()', making it odd, and increment it again upon unlocking, making it even. Readers sample the counter via 'read_seqbegin()' and retry the read if the sequence changed or was odd. Trap: seqlocks cannot protect pointers because writers can invalidate memory mid-read.
concepts.image_prompt: Loop diagram: Reader calls read_seqbegin, copies data, verifies read_seqretry; Writer enters write_seqlock (counter odd), modifies data, and exits (counter even); if sequence mismatch occurs, reader loops and retries.

concepts.title: Interrupt Handling: Top-Halves, Softirqs, and Threaded IRQs
concepts.content: Hardware interrupts execute the top-half handler with local interrupts disabled to acknowledge hardware immediately. Deferred work passes to bottom-halves: pre-allocated 'softirqs' (NET_RX, TIMER, RCU) or threaded IRQs created via 'request_threaded_irq()'. If softirqs consume excessive CPU cycles, the kernel delegates them to per-CPU 'ksoftirqd/X' daemons. Failure mode: unbounded top-half processing causes packet loss and severe audio/scheduling jitter.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline diagram: Hardware Interrupt triggers Top-Half handler (hardirq disabled), acknowledges hardware, raises Softirq; Softirq executes deferred work, overflowing into ksoftirqd kernel thread under heavy system load.

concepts.title: Kernel Timers: High-Resolution Timers (hrtimer) and NO_HZ
concepts.content: Legacy low-resolution timers rely on the periodic timer tick ('jiffies'). High-resolution timers ('hrtimers') use hardware timer counters (like HPET or LAPIC) to achieve nanosecond precision, organized in per-CPU red-black trees. In full tickless mode ('CONFIG_NO_HZ_FULL'), the kernel stops periodic ticks on isolated cores when only one runnable task exists, eliminating scheduling interruptions for latency-sensitive trading and simulation workloads.
concepts.image_prompt: Comparison matrix: Left diagram shows Periodic Jiffies Tick interrupting CPU every millisecond; Right diagram shows NO_HZ_FULL with red-black hrtimer tree scheduling single one-shot timer interrupt only when needed.

concepts.title: Virtual Filesystem (VFS): Inodes, Dentries, and Path Walking
concepts.content: The VFS abstracts heterogeneous storage formats using four core data structures: superblock, inode, dentry, and file. Directory hierarchies are cached in the 'dcache'. Path resolution traverses dentries using RCU-walk mode to achieve lock-free lookups. If memory lookup encounters missing or unvalidated dentries, it falls back to lock-heavy ref-walk. Trap: massive directory trees with millions of unique files evict dcache and saturate memory.
concepts.image_prompt: Tree diagram: Superblock points to root Inode; Dentry Cache tree maps directory paths to Inode metadata blocks, with RCU-walk path arrows resolving path lookups locklessly to open file descriptors.

concepts.title: Page Cache: Writeback Mechanics and Dirty Pages
concepts.content: Disk file I/O traverses the page cache unless opened with 'O_DIRECT'. Writes mark folios as dirty via 'set_page_dirty()'. Background kernel flushers write dirty folios to disk when dirty memory exceeds 'vm.dirty_background_ratio'. If dirty pages exceed 'vm.dirty_ratio', user threads throttle and block on synchronous I/O. Tip: tune 'dirty_writeback_centisecs' to prevent multi-gigabyte disk flushing write stalls.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline diagram: User process writes to File; data enters Page Cache Folios; Folio marked Dirty; background flusher flushes to disk past vm.dirty_background_ratio; synchronous throttling blocks user writes past vm.dirty_ratio.

concepts.title: Block I/O Layer: Multi-Queue Architecture (blk-mq)
concepts.content: The modern Linux block layer uses 'blk-mq' to eliminate global request lock contention on high-speed NVMe storage. It features two-tiered queueing: per-CPU software staging queues map to multiple hardware dispatch queues supported by the controller. I/O schedulers like 'none' (for NVMe) or 'kyber' mediate queue depth. Trap: misconfigured IRQ affinities pin all NVMe completion interrupts to CPU 0, creating a bottleneck.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline diagram: Per-CPU Software Staging Queues (Core 0..N) funnel BIO requests through blk-mq mapping layer into Hardware Dispatch Queues (H/W Queue 0..M), directly submitting to NVMe Storage Controller.

concepts.title: Asynchronous I/O: The io_uring Ring Buffer Engine
concepts.content: Created to replace slow POSIX AIO, 'io_uring' uses two ring buffers shared between user space and kernel space: the Submission Queue (SQ) and Completion Queue (CQ). By communicating via atomic head/tail pointers, operations require zero system calls in polling mode ('IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL'). Trap: submitting linked requests without checking error flags causes chained operations to execute unexpectedly after partial failures.
concepts.image_prompt: Loop diagram: Shared memory ring showing Submission Queue (SQ) where user app enqueues SQEs, Kernel Worker consumes and processes operations, and Completion Queue (CQ) where kernel posts CQEs for user consumption.

concepts.title: Network Packet Ingress: NAPI Polling and SKB Lifecycle
concepts.content: When network cards receive packets, hardware rings generate an interrupt triggering the driver top-half. The driver schedules a NAPI poll instance and disables device interrupts. The kernel processes incoming packets in batches up to 'netdev_max_backlog' using 'netif_receive_skb()', allocating a 'struct sk_buff'. Trap: oversized socket buffers and excessive backlog settings trigger bufferbloat and latency spikes under sustained load.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline diagram: Network NIC ring receives frames, fires single HardIRQ, transitions to NAPI Polling Loop; batch allocates sk_buff packets, processes protocol handlers, and returns to IRQ mode when ring empties.

concepts.title: Kernel Network Bypass: eXpress Data Path (XDP)
concepts.content: XDP executes sandboxed eBPF bytecode directly inside the network driver before 'sk_buff' allocation or TCP/IP stack overhead. Return codes dictate packet fate: 'XDP_DROP' discards malicious packets at wire speed, 'XDP_TX' bounces them back out the same NIC, and 'XDP_REDIRECT' routes frames into AF_XDP zero-copy user-space ring buffers. Trap: drivers lacking native XDP support fall back to slower generic driver hooks.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline diagram: Raw network packet hits NIC DMA buffer; XDP eBPF program runs instantly, branching into XDP_DROP (discard), XDP_TX (reflect), XDP_REDIRECT (AF_XDP socket), or standard Linux SKB network stack.

concepts.title: Stateful Packet Inspection: Netfilter and Connection Tracking
concepts.content: Netfilter provides five packet filtering hooks: PREROUTING, LOCAL_IN, FORWARD, LOCAL_OUT, and POSTROUTING. The connection tracking engine ('nf_conntrack') monitors bidirectional flows using hash tables. If conntrack tables fill up, the kernel drops new connections immediately with 'nf_conntrack: table full'. Mitigate by tuning 'net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max' and configuring 'NOTRACK' raw table rules for stateless, high-throughput proxies.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline diagram: Network packet traverses Netfilter hooks: PREROUTING flows into routing decision, splitting to LOCAL_IN (local process) or FORWARD; LOCAL_OUT merges to POSTROUTING, tracked by central nf_conntrack state table.

concepts.title: Userspace Synchronization: Futexes and futex2/futex_waitv
concepts.content: A Fast Userspace Mutex (futex) handles uncontended locking entirely in user space via atomic CAS. When contention occurs, the thread invokes 'futex(2)' to sleep on a kernel hash bucket queue. Linux 5.16+ introduced 'futex_waitv(2)', allowing a thread to wait on multiple futexes simultaneously—essential for Windows NT compatibility in Proton. Trap: priority inversion occurs unless using 'FUTEX_LOCK_PI' with kernel-managed 'rt_mutex' backing.
concepts.image_prompt: Comparison matrix: Left diagram shows Uncontended Futex executing atomic CAS entirely in User Space; Right diagram shows Contended Futex issuing futex_wait syscall to sleep in kernel wait-queue bucket.

concepts.title: Kernel Programmability: eBPF Verification and JIT Compilation
concepts.content: eBPF runs custom bytecode inside the kernel without recompiling code or loading dangerous modules. Before execution, the in-kernel verifier performs static analysis, checking for uninitialized registers, out-of-bounds pointer arithmetic, and guaranteeing loop termination. Validated programs are JIT-compiled into native machine instructions. Trap: complex multi-branch verifier state explosions can cause the kernel to reject valid eBPF programs during verification.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline diagram: C/BPF code compiles to eBPF Bytecode; Kernel Verifier validates safety, memory bounds, and termination; JIT Compiler emits native machine code; execution binds to Kernel Tracepoints and Maps.

concepts.title: Kernel Security: Linux Security Modules (LSM) and Landlock
concepts.content: The LSM framework provides security hooks throughout the kernel, mediating access to inodes, tasks, and network sockets via SELinux, AppArmor, or BPF LSM. 'Landlock' allows unprivileged processes to sandbox themselves by defining tailored filesystem and network restriction rulesets using 'landlock_restrict_self()'. Trap: stacked LSM modules evaluate sequentially; a single module returning '-EACCES' rejects the operation regardless of other policies.
concepts.image_prompt: Layered stack diagram: User Process system call enters VFS/Socket layer, passing sequentially through LSM Hook checks (SELinux, AppArmor, Landlock rules); if all grant permission, execution proceeds to underlying Kernel Subsystem.

concepts.title: Hardware-Assisted Virtualization: KVM and Hardware VMCS
concepts.content: Kernel-based Virtual Machine (KVM) turns Linux into a Type-1 hypervisor via '/dev/kvm'. The guest runs in VMX non-root operation using hardware CPU virtualization. When the guest executes privileged instructions or causes page faults, hardware triggers a 'VM-Exit' back to root mode. Hardware Extended Page Tables (EPT) handle guest-physical to host-physical translation. Trap: excessive VM-Exits collapse virtualization performance.
concepts.image_prompt: State diagram: Host Kernel runs in VMX Root Mode; executes VMLAUNCH/VMRESUME entering Guest VM in Non-Root Mode; Guest executes privileged instruction triggering hardware VM-Exit back to Host KVM handler.

concepts.title: Resource Control: cgroups v2 and Pressure Stall Information
concepts.content: Cgroups v2 provides a single unified hierarchy enforcing resource limits across CPU, memory, and I/O. Paired with Pressure Stall Information (PSI), administrators inspect '/proc/pressure/{cpu,memory,io}' to measure productive execution lost to resource starvation ('some' versus 'full' stall metrics). Tip: trigger early OOM intervention daemons like 'systemd-oomd' using PSI memory pressure event thresholds before system lockups occur.
concepts.image_prompt: Tree diagram: Unified cgroup v2 root tree with parent/child slices controlling memory.max, cpu.weight, and io.max; PSI sensors feed some/full starvation percentages to userspace systemd-oomd supervisor.

concepts.title: Namespace Isolation: Mount Topologies and Mount API
concepts.content: Linux namespaces (PID, NET, MNT, IPC, UTS, USER, CGROUP) isolate system resources for container runtimes. Mount propagation types ('MS_SHARED', 'MS_PRIVATE', 'MS_SLAVE') determine whether mount and unmount events replicate across mount namespaces. The modern Mount API ('fsopen', 'fsconfig', 'fsmount', 'move_mount') replaces monolithic 'mount(2)', preventing file descriptor leaks and path-walking race vulnerabilities. Common pitfall: unintended MS_SHARED mounts leak host storage inside container trees.
concepts.image_prompt: Comparison matrix: Left diagram shows MS_SHARED propagating mount events bidirectionally between host and container namespaces; Right diagram shows MS_PRIVATE isolating mount events strictly to the local namespace.

concepts.title: Dynamic Kernel Tracing: Ftrace, Kprobes, and eBPF Tracepoints
concepts.content: Ftrace instruments function calls using compiler-generated 'mcount' or 'fentry' hooks, dynamically patched with 'NOP' or trampoline instructions. 'Kprobes' enables dynamic tracing of arbitrary kernel instructions by replacing target opcodes with breakpoint traps ('int3' on x86). In contrast, static tracepoints use jump labels for zero-overhead inactive probing. Trap: placing kprobes on non-reentrant kernel routines or critical spinlock paths causes catastrophic recursion crashes.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline diagram: Target Kernel Function with fentry stub; if disabled, executes NOP; if enabled, redirects execution to Ftrace trampoline; alternative Kprobe replaces opcode with int3 trap, notifying debugger/eBPF probe.

concepts.title: Hardware Vulnerability Mitigation: Retpolines and Speculative Barriers
concepts.content: Transient execution attacks like Spectre exploit branch target buffers (BTB) to access unauthorized memory speculatively. The kernel mitigates indirect branch poisoning using 'retpolines'—trampolines that trap the CPU in an infinite pause loop during speculative execution. Modern processors use Enhanced IBRS (eIBRS) or FineIBT hardware features. Trade-off: speculative execution mitigations introduce 2-15% execution slowdowns, particularly on high-syscall workloads.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipeline diagram: Indirect Call instruction redirects into Retpoline trampoline; speculative branch predictor enters deliberate pause loop (speculation trap); CPU completes memory resolution and jumps safely to true target address.
